paragraphs: The Americans never use the word “peasant,” because they have no idea of the distinct class that the word describes. The ignorance of earlier ages, the simplicity of country life, and the rustic manners of the villager have not survived among them. They are equally strangers to the virtues, the vices, the coarse habits, and the simple graces of an early stage of civilization. At the far borders of the Confederate States, where society meets the wilderness, a population of bold adventurers has settled. They push into the solitude of the American forests and look for a new country there, to escape the poverty that awaited them in their native provinces. As soon as the pioneer reaches the spot that is to be his refuge, he fells a few trees and builds a log house. Nothing could look more wretched than these isolated dwellings. A traveler who approaches one of them toward nightfall sees the flicker of the hearth fire through the chinks in the walls. At night, if the wind rises, he hears the roof of boughs shaking to and fro among the great forest trees. Who would not take this poor hut for a refuge of crudeness and ignorance? Yet no comparison can be drawn between the pioneer and the dwelling that shelters him. Everything around him is primitive and unformed, but he himself is the product of the labor and experience of eighteen centuries. He dresses and speaks like the people of the cities. He knows the past, is curious about the future, and is ready to argue about the present. In short, he is a highly civilized man who agrees, for a time, to live in the backwoods, and who enters the wilds of the New World with a Bible, an axe, and a bundle of newspapers.

It is hard to imagine the incredible speed with which public opinion travels in the middle of these deserts. *j I do not think that so much intellectual exchange takes place even in the most educated and populous districts of France. *k There can be no doubt that, in the United States, the education of the people contributes powerfully to the support of a democratic republic. I believe this must always be so where education that awakens the understanding is not separated from moral training that improves the heart. But I do not exaggerate this benefit at all, and I am even further from thinking, as so many people in Europe do, that men can be turned into citizens at once by teaching them to read and write. True knowledge comes mainly from experience. If the Americans had not been gradually accustomed to governing themselves, their book learning would not help them much today.

j [ I traveled along part of the frontier of the United States in a kind of cart that was called the mail. We went on day and night, very fast, along roads that were barely marked out, through immense forests. When the darkness of the woods became impenetrable, the driver lit branches of fir, and we went on by the light they cast. From time to time we came to a hut in the middle of the forest, which was a post office. The mail dropped an enormous bundle of letters at the door of this isolated dwelling, and we continued at full gallop, leaving the people of the neighboring log houses to send for their share of the treasure.

[When the author visited America the locomotive and the railroad were scarcely invented, and not yet introduced in the United States. It is superfluous to point out the immense effect of those inventions in extending civilization and developing the resources of that vast continent. In 1831 there were 51 miles of railway in the United States; in 1872 there were 60,000 miles of railway.]]

k [ In 1832 each inhabitant of Michigan paid a sum equivalent to 1 fr. 22 cent. (French money) to the post-office revenue, and each inhabitant of the Floridas paid 1 fr. 5 cent. (See “National Calendar,” 1833, p. 244.) In the same year each inhabitant of the Departement du Nord paid 1 fr. 4 cent. to the revenue of the French post office. (See the “Compte rendu de l’administration des Finances,” 1833, p. 623.) Now the State of Michigan contained at that time only 7 inhabitants per square league and Florida only 5. The public education and the commercial activity of these districts are inferior to those of most of the States in the Union, while the Departement du Nord, which contains 3,400 inhabitants per square league, is one of the most educated and manufacturing parts of France.]

I have lived a great deal among the people of the United States, and I cannot say how much I admire their experience and their good sense. An American should never be allowed to speak of Europe, for then he will probably show a great deal of presumption and very foolish pride. He will fall back on those crude and vague ideas that are so useful to ignorant people all over the world. But if you ask him about his own country, the cloud that dimmed his intelligence lifts at once. His language becomes as clear and precise as his thoughts. He will tell you what his rights are and how he exercises them. He can point out the customs that prevail in the political world. You will find that he knows the rules of the administration well and is familiar with the workings of the laws. The citizen of the United States does not get his practical knowledge and his firm ideas from books. The schooling he has received may have prepared him to take in those ideas, but it did not supply them. The American learns the laws by taking part in making them, and he learns the forms of government by governing. The great work of society is always going on before his eyes and, as it were, under his hands.

In the United States, politics is the end and aim of education. In Europe, its main purpose is to fit men for private life. Citizens there take part in public affairs too rarely for education to anticipate it. A glance over society in the two hemispheres shows these differences even in its outward appearance.

In Europe we often carry the ideas and habits of private life into public affairs. Since we pass at once from the family circle to the government of the State, we can often be heard discussing the great interests of society in the same way we talk with our friends. The Americans, on the other hand, carry the habits of public life over into their private manners. In their country the jury system is brought into the games of schoolboys, and parliamentary rules are followed at the order of a feast.
The Laws Contribute More to the Maintenance of the Democratic Republic in the United States Than the Physical Circumstances of the Country, and the Manners More Than the Laws

All the nations of America have a democratic state of society — Yet democratic institutions survive only among the Anglo-Americans — The Spaniards of South America, as favored by physical causes as the Anglo-Americans, are unable to maintain a democratic republic — Mexico, which has adopted the Constitution of the United States, is in the same situation — The Anglo-Americans of the West are less able to maintain it than those of the East — The reason for these different results.

I have observed that the maintenance of democratic institutions in the United States is due to the circumstances, the laws, and the manners of that country. *l Most Europeans know only the first of these three causes, and they tend to give it a decisive importance that it does not really have.
l [ Let me remind the reader what I mean by the word “manners” in general: the moral and intellectual characteristics of men living in society, considered as a whole.]

It is true that the Anglo-Saxons settled in the New World in a state of social equality. The low-born and the noble were not to be found among them, and prejudices of profession were always as completely unknown as prejudices of birth. Thus, since the condition of society was democratic, the rule of democracy was established without difficulty. But this circumstance is by no means unique to the United States. Almost all the colonies across the Atlantic were founded by men who were equal among themselves, or who became so by settling there. In no part of the New World have Europeans been able to create an aristocracy. Nevertheless, democratic institutions prosper nowhere but in the United States.

The American Union has no enemies to contend with; it stands in the wilderness like an island in the ocean. But the Spaniards of South America were no less isolated by nature, and yet their position has not spared them the burden of standing armies. They make war on each other when they have no foreign enemies to fight. The Anglo-American democracy is the only one that has so far been able to maintain itself in peace. *m
m [ [A remark which, since the great Civil War of 1861-65, ceases to be applicable.]]

The territory of the Union offers a boundless field to human activity and inexhaustible materials for industry and labor. The passion for wealth takes the place of ambition, and the heat of faction is cooled by a sense of prosperity. But where in the world shall we find more fertile plains, mightier rivers, or richer and more unexplored resources than in South America?

Nevertheless, South America has been unable to maintain democratic institutions. If the welfare of nations depended on being placed in a remote position, with an unlimited expanse of habitable land before them, the Spaniards of South America would have no reason to complain of their lot. They might enjoy less prosperity than the inhabitants of the United States, and still their situation might be one that some nations in Europe would envy. Yet there are no nations on earth more miserable than those of South America.

Thus physical causes are not only unable to produce results like those that occur in North America; they cannot even raise the population of South America to the level of the States of Europe, where they work in the opposite direction. Physical causes, therefore, do not affect the destiny of nations as much as has been supposed.

I have met men in New England who were about to leave a country where they could have stayed in comfortable circumstances, in order to seek their fortune in the wilds. Not far from that region I found a French population in Canada, crowded into a narrow territory although the same wilds were close at hand. While the emigrant from the United States bought a large estate with the earnings of a short period of labor, the Canadian paid as much for land as he would have paid in France. Nature offers the solitudes of the New World to Europeans, but they do not always know how to turn her gifts to account. Other peoples of America have the same physical conditions for prosperity as the Anglo-Americans, but without their laws and their manners, and these peoples are wretched. The laws and manners of the Anglo-Americans are therefore the effective cause of their greatness, which is the object of my inquiry.

I am far from supposing that the American laws are excellent in themselves. I do not hold them to be applicable to all democratic peoples, and several of them seem dangerous to me, even in the United States. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that American legislation, taken as a whole, is extremely well suited to the genius of the people and the nature of the country it is meant to govern. The American laws are therefore good, and to them must be attributed a large share of the success of democratic government in America. But I do not believe they are the principal cause of that success. And if they seem to me to have more influence on the social happiness of the Americans than the nature of the country, there is, on the other hand, reason to believe that their effect is still less than that of the manners of the people.

The Federal laws are undoubtedly the most important part of the legislation of the United States. Mexico, which is no less fortunately situated than the Anglo-American Union, has adopted the same laws, yet it cannot accustom itself to democratic government. Some other cause is therefore at work, besides the physical circumstances and the particular laws that enable democracy to rule in the United States.

Another, still more striking proof can be offered. Almost all the inhabitants of the territory of the Union descend from a common stock. They speak the same language, they worship God in the same way, they are affected by the same physical causes, and they obey the same laws. Where, then, do their characteristic differences come from? Why, in the Eastern States of the Union, does republican government show vigor and regularity and proceed with mature deliberation? Where does it get the wisdom and the durability that mark its acts, while in the Western States, on the contrary, society seems to be ruled by chance? There, public business is conducted with an irregularity, and with a passionate and feverish excitement, that does not promise a long or secure life.

I am no longer comparing the Anglo-American States with foreign nations. I am contrasting them with each other and trying to discover why they are so unlike. The arguments drawn from the nature of the country and from differences in legislation are all set aside here. Some other cause must be found, and what other cause can there be except the manners of the people?

It is in the Eastern States that the Anglo-Americans have been longest accustomed to democratic government, and that they have formed the habits and conceived the ideas most favorable to its maintenance. Democracy has gradually penetrated their customs, their opinions, and the forms of social life. It is found in all the details of daily life as much as in the laws. In the Eastern States the education and practical training of the people have been most fully developed, and religion has been most thoroughly joined with liberty. Now these habits, opinions, customs, and convictions are precisely the elements of what I have called manners.

In the Western States, by contrast, part of these same advantages is still lacking. Many of the Americans of the West were born in the woods, and they mix the ideas and customs of savage life with the civilization of their parents. Their passions are more intense, their religious morality has less authority, and their convictions are less secure. The inhabitants exercise no control over their fellow citizens, for they scarcely know each other. The nations of the West show, to a certain extent, the inexperience and the rough habits of a people in its infancy. For although they are made up of old elements, their coming together is recent.

The manners of the Americans of the United States are, then, the real reason why that people alone, among the American nations, is able to sustain a democratic government. It is the influence of manners that produces the different degrees of order and prosperity that can be seen in the several Anglo-American democracies. Thus Europe exaggerates the effect that the geographical position of a country may have on the duration of democratic institutions. Too much importance is given to legislation, too little to manners. These three great causes no doubt serve to regulate and direct the American democracy. But if they were to be ranked in their proper order, I should say that physical circumstances are less effective than the laws, and the laws are very subordinate to the manners of the people. I am convinced that the most advantageous situation and the best possible laws cannot maintain a constitution in spite of the manners of a country, while manners can turn the most unfavorable situations and the worst laws to some advantage. The importance of manners is a common truth to which study and experience constantly direct our attention. It may be regarded as a central point in the range of human observation, and the common end of all inquiry. I insist so seriously on this point that, if I have so far failed to make the reader feel the important influence I attribute to the practical experience, the habits, the opinions, in short the manners of the Americans, on the maintenance of their institutions, I have failed in the principal object of my work.
Whether Laws and Manners Are Sufficient to Maintain Democratic Institutions in Other Countries Besides America

The Anglo-Americans, if transported into Europe, would be obliged to modify their laws — A distinction must be made between democratic institutions and American institutions — Democratic laws may be conceived that are better than, or at least different from, those the American democracy has adopted — The example of America only proves that it is possible to regulate democracy with the help of manners and legislation.

I have asserted that the success of democratic institutions in the United States is more closely tied to the laws themselves and the manners of the people than to the nature of the country. But does it follow that the same causes would produce the same results if they were put to work elsewhere? And if the country is no adequate substitute for laws and manners, can laws and manners in their turn substitute for the country? It is easy to see that the elements needed to answer this question are lacking. There are other peoples in the New World besides the Anglo-Americans, and since these peoples are affected by the same physical circumstances, they can fairly be compared with them. But there are no nations outside America that have adopted the same laws and manners while lacking the physical advantages peculiar to the Anglo-Americans. No standard of comparison therefore exists, and we can only venture an opinion on this subject.

It appears to me, first, that a careful distinction must be made between the institutions of the United States and democratic institutions in general. When I think about the state of Europe, its mighty nations, its populous cities, its formidable armies, and the complex nature of its politics, I cannot suppose that even the Anglo-Americans, if they were transported to our hemisphere with their ideas, their religion, and their manners, could exist without considerably altering their laws. But a democratic nation can be imagined that is organized differently from the American people. It is not impossible to conceive a government truly founded on the will of the majority, but one in which the majority, holding back its natural leaning toward equality, would consent, for the sake of the order and stability of the State, to give a family or an individual all the prerogatives of the executive. A democratic society might exist in which the forces of the nation would be more centralized than they are in the United States. The people would have a less direct and less irresistible influence on public affairs, and yet every citizen, invested with certain rights, would take part, within his sphere, in the conduct of the government. My observations among the Anglo-Americans lead me to believe that democratic institutions of this kind, prudently introduced into society so as gradually to blend with the habits and become intermingled with the opinions of the people, might survive in other countries besides America. If the laws of the United States were the only democratic laws one could imagine, or the most perfect one could conceive, I should admit that the success of those institutions proves nothing about the success of democratic institutions in general, in a country less favored by natural circumstances. But the laws of America seem to me defective in several respects, and I can readily imagine others of the same general kind. So the particular advantages of that country do not prove that democratic institutions cannot succeed in a nation less favored by circumstances, if it is ruled by better laws.

Suppose human nature were different in America from what it is elsewhere. Or suppose the social condition of the Americans produced among them habits and opinions different from those that arise from the same social condition in the Old World. Then the American democracies would give us no means of predicting what may happen in other democracies. Suppose the Americans showed the same propensities as all other democratic nations, and their legislators had relied on the nature of the country and the favor of circumstances to keep those propensities within proper limits. Then the prosperity of the United States would be attributable entirely to physical causes, and it would give no encouragement to a people inclined to imitate their example without sharing their natural advantages. But neither of these suppositions is borne out by the facts.

In America the same passions are found as in Europe, some arising from human nature, others from the democratic condition of society. Thus in the United States I found that restlessness of heart which is natural to men when all ranks are nearly equal and the chances of rising are the same for everyone. I found the democratic feeling of envy expressed in a thousand different forms. I noticed that the people often showed, in the conduct of affairs, a complete mixture of ignorance and presumption, and I concluded that in America men are subject to the same failings and the same absurdities as among ourselves. But when I examined the state of society more closely, I soon discovered that the Americans had made great and successful efforts to counteract these imperfections of human nature and to correct the natural defects of democracy. Their various municipal laws seemed to me a means of keeping the ambition of the citizens within a narrow sphere, and of turning those same passions that might have wreaked havoc in the State to the good of the township or the parish. The American legislators have succeeded, to a certain extent, in setting the notion of rights against the feelings of envy; the stability of the religious world against the constant shifting of politics; the experience of the people against its theoretical ignorance; and its practical knowledge of business against the impatience of its desires.

The Americans, then, have not relied on the nature of their country to counterbalance the dangers that arise from their Constitution and their political laws. To evils common to all democratic peoples they have applied remedies that no one but themselves had ever thought of before. Although they were the first to make the experiment, they have succeeded in it.

The manners and laws of the Americans are not the only ones that may suit a democratic people. But the Americans have shown that it would be wrong to despair of regulating democracy with the help of manners and laws. Suppose other nations borrow this general and fruitful idea from the Americans, without intending to imitate them in the particular way they have applied it. Suppose they try to fit themselves for the social condition that it seems to be the will of Providence to impose on the generations of this age, and so to escape the despotism or the anarchy that threatens them. What reason is there to suppose that their efforts would not be crowned with success? The organization and establishment of democracy in Christendom is the great political problem of the time. The Americans, unquestionably, have not solved this problem, but they supply useful data to those who undertake the task.
Importance of What Precedes With Respect to the State of Europe

It is easy to see with what intention I undertook the foregoing inquiries. The question discussed here interests not only the United States but the whole world. It concerns not one nation but all mankind. If nations whose social condition is democratic could remain free only as long as they lived in the wilds, we could only despair of the future destiny of the human race. For democracy is rapidly gaining wider sway, and the wilds are gradually being filled with people. If it were true that laws and manners are not enough to maintain democratic institutions, what refuge would remain open to nations except the despotism of a single individual? I am aware that there are many worthy people at the present time who are not alarmed by this alternative, and who are so tired of liberty that they would be glad of rest, far from the storms that accompany it. But these people do not know well the harbor toward which they are headed. They are so deceived by their memories that they judge the tendency of absolute power by what it was in the past, and not by what it might become today.

If absolute power were re-established among the democratic nations of Europe, I am persuaded that it would take a new form and appear with features unknown to our forefathers. There was a time in Europe when the laws and the consent of the people had given princes almost unlimited authority, but they hardly ever made use of it. I do not speak of the prerogatives of the nobility, of the authority of the supreme courts of justice, of corporations and their chartered rights, or of provincial privileges. These served to soften the blows of the sovereign authority and to keep a spirit of resistance alive in the nation. Apart from these political institutions, which however opposed they may have been to personal liberty served to keep the love of freedom alive in the public mind, and which may be considered useful in that respect, the manners and opinions of the nation confined royal authority within barriers that were no less powerful for being less conspicuous. Religion, the affections of the people, the kindness of the prince, the sense of honor, family pride, provincial prejudices, custom, and public opinion all limited the power of kings and held their authority within an invisible circle. The constitution of nations was despotic at that time, but their manners were free. Princes had the right, but they had neither the means nor the desire, to do whatever they pleased.

But what remains now of those barriers that once stopped the aggressions of tyranny? Religion has lost its empire over the souls of men, so the most prominent boundary between good and evil has been overthrown. The very elements of the moral world are uncertain. The princes and the peoples of the earth are guided by chance, and no one can define the natural limits of despotism or the bounds of license. Long revolutions have destroyed forever the respect that once surrounded the rulers of the State. Now that they have been relieved of the burden of public esteem, princes may from now on give themselves up without fear to the temptations of arbitrary power.

When kings find that the hearts of their subjects are turned toward them, they are merciful, because they are conscious of their strength. They are careful of the affection of their people, because that affection is the bulwark of the throne. A mutual exchange of goodwill then takes place between the prince and the people, like the gracious relations of a family. The subjects may grumble at the sovereign’s decree, but they are grieved to displease him, and the sovereign punishes his subjects with the light hand of parental affection.

But once the spell of royalty is broken in the tumult of revolution, and successive monarchs have passed across the throne, alternately showing the people the weakness of their right and the harshness of their power, the sovereign is no longer regarded by anyone as the Father of the State, and he is feared by all as its master. If he is weak, he is despised. If he is strong, he is hated. He himself is full of animosity and alarm. He finds that he is a stranger in his own country, and he treats his subjects like conquered enemies.

When the provinces and the towns formed so many different nations within their common country, each of them had a will of its own, opposed to the general spirit of subjection. But now all the parts of the same empire have lost their immunities, their customs, their prejudices, their traditions, and their names, and have been subjected and accustomed to the same laws. It is no more difficult to oppress them all together than it was once to oppress them one by one.

While the nobles held their power, and indeed long after they had lost it, the honor of aristocracy gave extraordinary force to their personal opposition. There are instances of men who, despite their weakness, still held a high opinion of their personal worth and dared to stand alone against the efforts of the public authority. But today all ranks are more and more mixed together, the individual disappears in the crowd and is easily lost in a common obscurity, the honor of monarchy has almost lost its empire without being replaced by public virtue, and nothing enables a man to rise above himself. Who can say at what point the demands of power and the servility of weakness will stop?

As long as family feeling was kept alive, the opponent of oppression was never alone. He looked around him and found his clients, his hereditary friends, and his relatives. If this support was lacking, he was sustained by his ancestors and inspired by his descendants. But when inherited estates are divided, and a few years are enough to blur the distinctions of a race, where can family feeling be found? What force can there be in the customs of a country that has changed and is still constantly changing its aspect? In such a country every act of tyranny has a precedent and every crime an example. There is nothing so old that its antiquity can save it from destruction, and nothing so unparalleled that its novelty can prevent it from being done. What resistance can be offered by manners so pliant that they have already often yielded? What strength can even public opinion have kept, when no twenty persons are connected by a common tie? When not a man, nor a family, nor a chartered corporation, nor a class, nor a free institution has the power to represent or assert that opinion? When every citizen, equally weak, equally poor, and equally dependent, has only his personal helplessness to oppose to the organized force of the government?

The annals of France offer nothing like the condition into which that country might then be thrown. It may more fittingly be compared to the times of old, to those hideous eras of Roman oppression, when the manners of the people were corrupted, their traditions wiped out, their habits destroyed, and their opinions shaken. Freedom, driven out of the laws, could find no refuge in the land. Nothing protected the citizens, and the citizens no longer protected themselves. Human nature was the plaything of man, and princes wore out the mercy of Heaven before they exhausted the patience of their subjects. Those who hope to revive the monarchy of Henry IV or of Louis XIV seem to me to be afflicted with mental blindness. When I consider the present condition of several European nations, a condition toward which all the others are tending, I am led to believe that they will soon be left with no other alternative than democratic liberty or the tyranny of the Caesars. *n
n [ [This prediction of the return of France to imperial despotism, and of the true character of that despotic power, was written in 1832, and realized to the letter in 1852.]]

And indeed it deserves consideration whether men are to be entirely emancipated or entirely enslaved, whether their rights are to be made equal or wholly taken away from them. Suppose the rulers of society were reduced either to raising the crowd gradually to their own level or to pushing the citizens below the level of humanity. Would not the doubts of many be resolved, the consciences of many be healed, and the community be prepared to make great sacrifices with little difficulty? In that case, the gradual growth of democratic manners and institutions should be regarded not as the best means of preserving freedom but as the only one. Even without liking democratic government, one might adopt it as the most workable and the fairest remedy for the present ills of society.

It is difficult to draw a people into the work of government, but it is still more difficult to give it the experience and to inspire in it the feelings it needs in order to govern well. I grant that the caprices of democracy are perpetual, its instruments crude, its laws imperfect. But suppose it were true that soon no just middle ground would exist between the empire of democracy and the dominion of a single arm. Should we not rather incline toward the former than submit voluntarily to the latter? And if complete equality is to be our fate, is it not better to be leveled by free institutions than by despotic power?

Anyone who, after reading this book, imagines that I wrote it to propose the laws and manners of the Anglo-Americans for the imitation of all democratic peoples would make a very great mistake. Such a reader must have paid more attention to the form than to the substance of my ideas. My aim has been to show, by the example of America, that there may be laws, and especially manners, that allow a democratic people to remain free. But I am very far from thinking that we ought to follow the example of the American democracy and copy the means it has used to reach its ends. I am well aware of the influence that the nature of a country and its political precedents have on a constitution, and I should regard it as a great misfortune for mankind if liberty were to exist all over the world in the same forms.

But I am of the opinion that if we do not succeed in gradually introducing democratic institutions into France, and if we despair of giving the citizens those ideas and feelings that first prepare them for freedom and then allow them to enjoy it, there will be no independence at all, neither for the middle classes nor the nobility, neither for the poor nor the rich, but an equal tyranny over all. And I foresee that if the peaceable empire of the majority is not founded among us in time, we shall sooner or later arrive at the unlimited authority of a single despot.
